q: Model-free vs model-based RL?
short: Model-free learns values or policies directly from real experience; model-based learns or is given a model of transitions/rewards and uses it to plan, usually gaining sample efficiency at the risk of model errors.

q: Distribution vs sample models?
short: A distribution model gives all next states/rewards with probabilities (needed for DP's expected updates); a sample model returns one sampled outcome (simulators, game rules, learned networks), easier to obtain.
mistakes: Calling a simulator a distribution model.

q: Describe Dyna-Q.
short: Each real step: Q-learning update from the real transition, store (R, S′) for (S, A) in the model, then n planning updates on randomly chosen remembered (S, A) pairs using the model's outcome.
detail: Learning and planning share the same update.

q: What problem does Dyna-Q+ solve?
short: Out-of-date models in changing environments, especially optimistic shortcuts the model doesn't know about; a bonus κ√τ for long-untried transitions makes the agent re-test them.

q: What are the four phases of MCTS?
short: Selection (follow UCB1 down the tree), expansion (add a child), simulation (rollout to the end with a default policy), backup (update visit counts and values along the path).
mistakes: Forgetting perspective flips in two-player backup.

q: AlphaGo vs AlphaGo Zero?
short: AlphaGo: supervised policy from human games, RL policy, value network, MCTS with rollouts. AlphaGo Zero: no human data, single policy–value network trained from self-play with MCTS as policy improvement, no rollouts; stronger.
follow: What does MCTS provide during training?

q: What is model bias?
short: Systematic errors in a learned model that a planner exploits (finding imagined high-reward trajectories that don't exist), worsened by compounding error over long imagined rollouts.
mistakes: Assuming more planning is always better.

q: Why does planning speed up the maze so much?
short: After the first episode only the final transition has value; each planning update can propagate value one step backwards through remembered transitions, so with n = 50 most of the path gains value before the next real step instead of one state per episode.
follow: How does prioritised sweeping improve on this?

q: Background planning vs decision-time planning?
short: Background planning (Dyna, DP) continually improves a global value function/policy used everywhere; decision-time planning (MCTS, rollouts) focuses computation on the current state to choose this action, then largely discards the tree.

q: How does AlphaZero use MCTS during training?
short: MCTS guided by the current network produces improved move distributions (visit counts); the network's policy head is trained toward them and its value head toward game outcomes, so search acts as a policy-improvement operator.
mistakes: Thinking the network is trained on human games.

q: Why may MCTS with random rollouts fail in deep positions?
short: Random playouts are noisy, weak estimates of a position's value when the game is long; win-rate differences between moves become tiny (Nim from 21: ~0.02), so many simulations are needed. Learned value networks or better default policies fix this.

q: What does MuZero learn and why is it notable?
short: A representation function (observation → latent), a dynamics function (latent, action → next latent, reward) and a prediction function (latent → policy, value), trained only to predict quantities relevant to planning; MCTS runs in the latent space without the true rules.
detail: Works on Atari and board games.

q: What is prioritised sweeping?
short: Planning updates are ordered by priority (expected size of value change, e.g. Bellman error); when a state's value changes, its predecessors are queued, so planning works backwards from changes efficiently.

q: Dyna vs experience replay in DQN?
short: Both reuse past transitions for extra updates; replay can be seen as a non-parametric sample model (stored real transitions). Dyna with a learned model can also generate transitions never actually experienced (if the model generalises).
detail: Replay ≈ Dyna with a memory model.
follow: When does a learned model help more?

q: You have an expensive robot but a decent simulator. How would you use model-based ideas?
short: Train primarily in simulation (sample model), use domain randomisation; on the robot, collect data to fit a residual/learned model and do short-horizon model rollouts (MBPO-style) mixed with real data; use ensembles to detect uncertainty and avoid exploiting model errors.

q: Why play the most-visited move rather than the highest-value move after MCTS?
short: Visit counts are robust: a child with a high mean from few visits may be noise; UCB already sends more visits to children that remain good, so visits reflect confidence-weighted quality.

q: How do ensembles help model-based RL?
short: Several models trained on the same data disagree where data are scarce; disagreement estimates epistemic uncertainty, so the planner can penalise or avoid uncertain regions and sample model rollouts across members, reducing exploitation of a single model's errors.
follow: How to use disagreement for exploration?

q: What does the compounding-error calculation show?
short: With per-step relative error e, an H-step imagined rollout can drift by (1 + e)^H − 1 in the worst case (5% over 20 steps ≈ 165%), so long model rollouts are unreliable; keep them short or re-ground with real observations.

q: How do model-based and model-free RL relate to GPI?
short: Both follow GPI: model-based uses simulated experience (planning) for evaluation/improvement, model-free uses real experience; Dyna shows they can share the same update rule and value function.
mistakes: Treating planning as unrelated to learning.
